headline: Claude Basecamp is now open-source: an OS for Claude Code, seeking collaborators
summary: This open-source OS aims to manage all Claude Code interactions, from repos to sessions, with features like a 'reconciliation loop' for always-green tests and session rescue. It runs locally with no install or config.
details: Claude Basecamp, an open-source operating system for Claude Code, has been released. It aims to consolidate all Claude Code interactions into one place, moving beyond scattered terminal windows and dead transcripts.

The project's initial feature is a "reconciliation loop" designed to ensure declared states, like "tests always green" or "dependencies current," remain true. It dispatches fixes and only prompts human intervention for critical decisions.
Basecamp requires no installation or configuration. It automatically discovers existing Claude Code projects and becomes accessible via http://localhost:4747, operating entirely locally.

It introduces "Reflexes" by analyzing past transcripts to identify instances where users corrected Claude Code. These become standing memories, preventing the same mistakes from recurring in future sessions.

The system also includes "Session Rescue," allowing users to resume dead Claude Code sessions with full context, avoiding restarts. It acts as a manager for repositories, tracking goals and providing an activity feed, GitHub integration, and notifications.

The developer is actively seeking collaborators to expand Basecamp's capabilities, including resource governors for token budgets, cost guardrails, and more routine templates. The goal is to make it the default environment for all Claude Code workflows.

Claude Basecamp is built with zero dependencies, approximately 4,000 lines of Node.js, and runs locally with no telemetry. It's read-only on Claude data except for explicit, confirmed write paths and is released under the Unlicense for maximum flexibility.
caption:

Claude Basecamp, an open-source operating system for Claude Code, has been released. It aims to consolidate all Claude Code interactions into one place, moving beyond scattered terminal windows and dead transcripts.

The project's initial feature is a "reconciliation loop" designed to ensure declared states, like "tests always green" or "dependencies current," remain true. It dispatches fixes and only prompts human intervention for critical decisions.

Basecamp requires no installation or configuration. It automatically discovers existing Claude Code projects and becomes accessible via http://localhost:4747, operating entirely locally.

It introduces "Reflexes" by analyzing past transcripts to identify instances where users corrected Claude Code. These become standing memories, preventing the same mistakes from recurring in future sessions.

The system also includes "Session Rescue," allowing users to resume dead Claude Code sessions with full context, avoiding restarts. It acts as a manager for repositories, tracking goals and providing an activity feed, GitHub integration, and notifications.

The developer is actively seeking collaborators to expand Basecamp's capabilities, including resource governors for token budgets, cost guardrails, and more routine templates. The goal is to make it the default environment for all Claude Code workflows.

Claude Basecamp is built with zero dependencies, approximately 4,000 lines of Node.js, and runs locally with no telemetry. It's read-only on Claude data except for explicit, confirmed write paths and is released under the Unlicense for maximum flexibility.

headline_marked: [[Netflix reportedly considers adding always-on channels]] and streaming bundles
headline: Netflix reportedly considers adding always-on channels and streaming bundles
summary: The streaming giant is exploring new strategies, including bundles with other services, to combat falling engagement and viewership drops for second seasons of its shows.
details: Netflix is reportedly exploring "always-on channels" that would stream specific shows and movies, similar to free ad-supported services like Pluto TV and Tubi. This strategy aims to counter signs of falling engagement, as reported by The Wall Street Journal.

The company is also considering offering bundles that would include other streaming services, a model already used by competitors such as Apple TV and Prime Video. These initiatives are part of a broader effort to reverse declining viewership.

This comes after a Bloomberg report highlighted significant viewership drops for second seasons of Netflix's original shows. Netflix has recently introduced new content types like video podcasts and digital media brand videos, which are easier to leave running in the background.

While free services like Pluto TV are ad-supported, Netflix's own ad-supported tier costs $8.99 per month after a recent price hike. The potential new channels could follow a similar model or be integrated into existing subscription tiers.
